title: Price tag plus running cost
hook: A higher upfront price can cross a lower one after repeated running costs.

knows: that a model can declare hypothetical quantities
doesNotKnow: Combine an upfront amount and repeated operating charges without assuming the same winner at every horizon.

misconception: The lower initial price guarantees a lower total at every future horizon.
objective: Combine an upfront amount and repeated operating charges without assuming the same winner at every horizon.

claims.text: Illustrative A costs €80 plus 120kWh/year. B costs €140 plus 60kWh/year. Electricity is €0.30/kWh. Scaled model; Illustrative costs: €80 plus 120 kWh/year, or €140 plus 60 kWh/year, at €0.30/kWh.
claims.source: Declared hypothetical inputs and limits in resource-specs.json. No actual product, price, tariff, shelf-life, treatment or physical appliance specification is asserted. claims.text: Illustrative A costs €80 plus 120kWh/year; B costs €140 plus 60kWh/year; electricity is a fictional €0.30/kWh. When does B's total become lower? Correct: After about 3.3 years. B starts €60 higher but saves 60kWh × €0.30 = €18 a year, so it catches up after €60 ÷ €18 ≈ 3.3 years.

claims.text: For a stated constant load, kWh = watts × hours ÷ 1000. Running cost = kWh × the stated price per kWh; stated fixed costs are added separately.
claims.source: https://www.energy.gov.au/households/energy-rating Australian Government, Energy Ratings, sections Electrical appliances without a star rating / Estimate running costs. Opened 2026-10-13. This supports the general calculation, not the invented model ratings or tariff. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Unit identity, re-derived: 1 kWh = 1,000 W × 1 h, so a constant load of W watts for h hours uses W·h/1000 kWh; a per-kWh tariff makes running cost = kWh × price, and fixed costs are added separately. The lesson model matches: A = 80 + 120 × 0.30 × years, B = 140 + 60 × 0.30 × years. The watts clause is not on this lesson's stage (it states kWh/year directly). energy.gov.au not opened; the claim does not rest on it. Nit (builder): support could be 'derivation'.

claims.note: FC pass 50 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened two sources myself. (1) Rokicki et al. (2021), 'Differentiation and Changes of Household Electricity Prices in EU Countries', Energies 14(21): 6894, DOI 10.3390/en14216894, publisher abstract read via api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/en14216894 (mdpi.com itself is blocked; abstract only, not full text): the paper sets out 'to identify the differentiation and variation of electricity prices for households in EU countries' (28 states, 2008-2019, Eurostat data) and finds 'higher electricity prices for households in the EU states were associated with better economic parameters', so household prices differ between countries. (2) OpenStax College Physics 2e, section 'Electric Power and Energy' (module m42714, raw.githubusercontent.com/openstax/osbooks-college-physics-bundle/main/modules/m42714/index.cnxml): 'We also think of lightbulbs in terms of their power ratings in watts. Together these carry 'Tariffs and appliance ratings vary'; 'check your own' is advice that follows from the OpenStax sentence. The line is hedged and claims no size.
